Venus holds a reputation for being one of the most dangerous planets out there. Hotter than even Mercury, and with a landscape featuring volcanoes, earthquakes, and other threats, Venus is a place that no one would ever think of living. However, that doesn't stop some. Although no mission has lasted for longer than a few hours on Venus, scientists continue to research to find better ways to study this desolate planet. The question is: is it worth it? Is it worth it to explore such a place? According to the author of "The Challenge of Exploring Venus," it is. The author makes the well-supported claim that, despite the dangers, the study and exploration of Venus is worth the risk.

The author makes several points to support his claim. First, the author points out that Venus is one of the closest planets to Earth, in addition to Mars. Because of the length of time required for space travel, it makes sense to focus on the planets closest to Earth. The less time it takes to travel to a destination, the more time can be spent there, researching and observing. Another point that the author makes is that Venus may have once been much more like Earth than it is now. A long time ago, Venus may have had oceans like ours, which could have supported life. Even today, Venus' geological features are very similar to Earth's--Venus has valleys, mountains, and craters, just like Earth does. Studying Venus could provide a deeper insight into the formation and geological history of our own planet. Finally, the author gives examples of how scientists are working on ways to overcome the harsh Venusian conditions long enough for meaningful observations to be made. One such approach is to have a blimp-like aircraft hover thirty miles or so above the ground. Up that far, temperatures would still be hot (about 170 degrees Fahrenheit), but they would be managable, and the air pressure and radiation levels would be like that of Earth. Other innovations, such as making simple electronics with silicon carbide or mechanical computers without any of the delicacy of modern electronics, are also being developed. Altogether, the points that the author makes are enough to convince anyone that the exploration of Venus is a worthy pursuit.

The mysteries that Venus holds can be uncovered with enough time and effort. As the author puts it, "human curiosity will likely lead us into many equally intimidating endeavors." The endeavor of overcoming Venus is intimidating indeed, but it is possible--it only needs to be done.
